newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy dairy farmers see progress in quota dispute.
newsitem.headline: Italy dairy farmers see progress in quota dispute.

text.p: Italian dairy farmers said on Monday they had made some progress in talks with Prime Minister Romano Prodi on a dispute over EU fines for milk overproduction but insisted they should not pay.

"By tonight or tomorrow, things should be clearer," Giovanni Robusti, a spokesman for one of the farmers' groups told reporters after nearly three hours of talks with Prodi and Agriculture Minister Michele Pinto.
"We've made some progress. There's time," he said.

The dispute, which has been accompanied by nearly two weeks of road blocks, centres on European Union "super-levy" fines, due to be paid by Friday, for overshooting Italy's national 1995-96 milk quota of 9.9 million tonnes by some 400,000 tonnes.
The fines add up to some 370 billion lire ($230 million).
Farmers want the government to pay the fines but Prodi has refused, offering cheap loans instead.
The government has suggested that a commission of inquiry should be set up to evaluate the situation, and that in the meantime the farmers should pay a first instalment of the fines.

Farmers, who say the government is to blame for miscalculating the quotas thus allowing them to overproduce, have welcomed the notion of a commission but do not agree that they should pay a tranche of the levy.
"The problem is not how we should pay but who should pay," said Robusti. "The levy should be paid by the person who is responsible for having produced it. And we don't think that is the farmers."
Mauro Carturani, another farming association leader present at the talks, doubted the dispute would be resolved on Monday.
"We've come along a short way," he said. "We've still got about 60 percent to go." But he said there was still time before Friday's deadline.
Farmers say that the fines would be ruinous and have taken to the roads up and down the country in their tractors to draw attention to their plight.
Milan's main Linate airport had to be shut briefly last week because farmers in tractors had barricaded the access routes.
Flag carrier Alitalia said it would sue the dairy farmers for damages to cover the billions of lire it said it had lost because of flight delays and cancellations.
Farmers dismantled blockades in the financial capital Milan ahead of the talks with Prodi but staged protests near Turin, at Verona and Venice airports and on a main southern motorway.
Prodi, who met the farmers last week for a first round of talks, ordered "all appropriate means" to be used to ensure that people and transport could move freely.
For several days last week, passengers had to walk more than a kilometre (0.6 mile) to Linate's terminal to catch flights.
Under the quota system, national farmers produce just over half of the 18 million tonnes of milk Italy consumes.
Pinto has formally asked the European Commission to raise Italy's quota to 10.5 million tonnes and has outlined a package of aid measures.
But the government says it cannot overlook the tens of thousands of farmers who have stuck to their quotas or have already paid up. ($1=1,595 lire)
